item.title: Strategic Brief — August 25, 2026: US Pushes Nationwide Arms Embargo on Sudan as Washington Prepares Largest Visa Revocation in History
item.description:
Washington escalates on two fronts: a UN Security Council push to expand Sudan's arms embargo nationwide, and a plan to revoke up to 200,000 visas from asylum-seekers. Meanwhile the US-Canada trade war deepens and new Iran sanctions target third countries.
The United States is pressing the UN Security Council to expand Sudan's arms embargo from Darfur to the entire country, in a bid to choke off the external support that has sustained a war now in its fourth year. Trump's senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, Massad Boulos, told the Security Council on Monday that financial, military and political backing for both the government forces and the rival Rapid Support Forces remains a driver of the conflict, which has killed at least 59,000 people and displaced some 13 million, according to AP. The proposed US resolution would apply the embargo to all parties operating in Sudan's territory and explicitly reaffirm that drones and related technologies fall under it. Boulos did not name the countries providing support, but AP notes Egypt has backed the military while UN experts and human rights groups have accused the UAE of arming the RSF, a charge Abu Dhabi denies.
The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum in the United States, according to State Department documents obtained by AP and two US officials. The move, coordinated with the Department of Homeland Security, would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history and would likely face legal challenges. State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott confirmed the coordination, saying the department is identifying and revoking the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who came as short-term visitors but then filed for asylum. He declined to give a number, calling the process ongoing and rolling. Officials said most of those with pending asylum cases would be recategorized but would lose their business or tourism status, though the revocations would not necessarily mean immediate deportation.
The United States imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian products early Saturday, and Canada said it would retaliate beginning September 8 after last-ditch negotiations failed to resolve the latest strain between the historic allies, AP reports. Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Canada's response on Parliament Hill, while President Donald Trump told Canadian leaders to 'fall in line.' The escalation follows the collapse of talks that had been meant to head off a new round of tariffs. The dispute now carries real economic weight on both sides of the border, hitting steel and other industrial goods at a moment when supply chains are already under strain.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced new sanctions on Monday aimed at blocking all potential sources of revenue for Iran, including secondary sanctions on countries that continue to do business with Tehran, according to AP. The Iranian rial dropped to 2.02 million to the dollar as trading opened, extending a slide that began well before the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February. Iran warned of a harsh response to the new measures. In a sign of Tehran's diplomatic maneuvering, Iran's Parliament Speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf met Pakistan's Army Chief Field Marshal Gen. Asim Munir in Tehran on Monday. The secondary sanctions are the sharpest escalation yet of Washington's economic campaign, threatening to force third countries to choose between the US financial system and trade with Iran.
Israeli police arrested a 16-year-old boy from the Israeli settlement of Avigayil in connection with the beating of a 61-year-old Palestinian man with a pipe in the occupied West Bank, AP reports. The arrest comes amid a broader pattern of settler violence that has drawn international criticism and added friction to US-Israel relations. The incident is a reminder that the West Bank remains a live flashpoint even as attention focuses on Gaza and the wider Iran confrontation, with settler attacks and Palestinian casualties continuing to feed instability in the territory.
Today's developments show Washington escalating on multiple fronts at once: a UN push to expand Sudan's arms embargo nationwide, the largest mass visa revocation in US history, a deepening tariff war with Canada, and new secondary sanctions on Iran that force third countries to pick a side. The common thread is an administration willing to use economic and legal leverage aggressively against adversaries and allies alike. The Iran sanctions and the Sudan embargo both aim to cut external support to hostile actors, while the visa and tariff moves signal a harder line on immigration and trade. The risk is that these parallel confrontations compound each other, stretching US attention and diplomatic capital across the Middle East, Africa, and North America simultaneously.

item.title: Strategic Brief — August 24, 2026: US Readies 'Most Crushing Economic Operation' Against Iran as Tehran Calls Sanctions Support an 'Act of War'
item.description:
Washington is shifting the Iran conflict from the battlefield to a coordinated economic-isolation campaign aimed at collapsing the regime, with details due today. Canada walked away from trade talks with the White House, and a new peace roadmap emerged for eastern DR Congo.
The defining shift today is Washington's decision to wage economic war on Iran — a coordinated isolation campaign aimed at collapsing the regime, with details due at a press conference on 24 August and Tehran warning that supporting it would be an 'act of war.' That escalation, alongside Canada's decision to walk away from trade talks with the US, points to a world where economic coercion has become the primary instrument of great-power pressure. Meanwhile, a credible peace roadmap emerged for eastern DR Congo, Ukraine's political crisis deepened over wartime elections, and Thailand's southern insurgency flared in a coordinated arson wave. The common thread: the tools of statecraft are shifting from the battlefield to the balance sheet, and every ally is being forced to pick a side.

item.title: Strategic Brief — August 23, 2026: US-Canada Trade War Escalates as Talks Collapse, Washington and Ankara Friction Grows Over Israeli Strikes in Syria
item.description:
Washington imposed 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods after negotiations collapsed, deepening a rupture in the Western alliance. Separately, a US envoy says Israel struck Syria without notice and may have been baiting Turkey, exposing strain inside the anti-Iran coalition.
The defining development of the day is the collapse of US-Canada talks into a 50 percent tariff war, marking the clearest economic rupture yet inside the Western alliance, while the US-led camp against Iran shows internal strain as Washington's envoy accuses Israel of provoking Turkey with strikes in Syria. Iran is widening its own threat to alternative oil routes in response to fresh US pressure, and the Russia-Ukraine drone war continues to escalate on both sides of the border. The broadest picture is one of simultaneous fragmentation, as economic, military and climate pressures erode alliances and supply chains once taken for granted.

item.title: Strategic Brief — August 22, 2026: Iran Threatens NATO's Southeast Flank as War Nears Europe, US-Pakistan Spat Erupts Over Kashmir Visit
item.description:
Tehran warns it will strike Bulgaria's Bezmer Air Base and other European targets aiding US operations, while Washington pivots from military to economic pressure on Iran. Separately, a Trump envoy's Kashmir visit strains US-Pakistan ties.
The Iran-US war is entering a new phase: Tehran is threatening NATO's European flank even as both sides signal openness to ending the conflict, with Washington pivoting to a sanctions campaign and Iran insisting it negotiates from strength. The US re-designation of Hezbollah as an Iranian proxy widens the legal and financial front, while a Trump envoy's Kashmir remarks strain US-Pakistan ties and Bangladesh holds its first contested presidential vote in decades. The central question is whether the war can be contained to the Middle East or whether Europe's southeast becomes the next front.

item.title: Strategic Brief — August 21, 2026: Iran Weighs Strikes on US Bases in Europe as War Threatens to Leap the Mediterranean, Israel Bombs Syrian Base to Block Turkish Deployment
item.description:
Iranian sources tell the FT the IRGC has assessed US bases across Europe — including in Bulgaria — as contingency targets if the conflict widens, a move that would drag NATO territory directly into a war so far confined to the Gulf. Separately, Israel struck the Abu al-Duhur airbase in Syria to prevent a Turkish deployment, opening a new Israel-Turkey flashpoint, while Russia killed at least 13 people in a nine-hour barrage on Kyiv.
The defining shift of the day is geographic: Iran's reported contingency planning against US bases in Europe would, if realized, turn a Gulf war into a direct challenge to NATO territory and the logistics spine that feeds both that fight and Ukraine. That prospect lands alongside a new Israel-Turkey confrontation over Syria — Israel bombing the Abu al-Duhur base to block a Turkish deployment and drawing an unusual public rebuke from Washington — a brutal Russian strike on Kyiv, a Gulf conflict now fought largely through sanctions and trade cutoffs, and mounting strain in the West Bank and Sudan. The wars that began in the Middle East and Eastern Europe are showing clear signs of merging — with Turkey's expanding Syria role and Europe's hollowed-out air defenses as the vulnerable hinges.
